drills.q: What three pointer variables does the iterative linked-list reversal technique use, and what is each one's job?
drills.a: prev (the new list built so far, starts null), curr (the node currently being rewired), and next_temp (a saved reference to curr's original next node, captured before curr.next is overwritten).

drills.q: What line must always execute before curr.next = prev, and what breaks if it doesn't?
drills.a: next_temp = curr.next must execute first. If curr.next is overwritten before saving it, you lose the only reference to the rest of the original list -- the traversal can no longer advance past the current node correctly.

drills.q: Derive why iterative reversal is O(1) space while recursive reversal of the same list is O(n) space, given both perform the identical set of pointer rewrites.
drills.a: Both approaches touch each node's next pointer exactly once, so both are O(n) time doing the same work. The difference is where intermediate state lives: iterative reversal uses three fixed scalar variables regardless of list length (O(1) space), while recursive reversal pushes one stack frame per node before any rewiring happens (since you recurse all the way to the tail before starting to fix pointers on the way back up), and those frames aren't released until the full unwind completes -- O(n) stack frames outstanding at the deepest point.

drills.q: Why is a dummy node placed before the head standard practice for Reverse Linked List II (reverse between positions left and right)?
drills.a: The splice-back step needs a pointer to the node immediately before position left, so it can be reconnected to the new head of the reversed segment. If left == 1, there is no real node before the range -- without a dummy node you'd need a special case for 'range starts at head'; the dummy node guarantees a predecessor always exists, eliminating that special case.

drills.q: In Reverse Nodes in k-Group (LC25), design the check that decides whether a group should be reversed, and explain why it must happen before reversing, not after.
drills.a: Before reversing a group, walk ahead k nodes from the group's start to confirm all k nodes exist (i.e., you don't run off the end of the list). If fewer than k nodes remain, stop and leave that final partial group in its original order, per LC25's spec. This check must happen before reversing because reversing first and then discovering a short group would require un-reversing it -- extra, avoidable work and a common source of bugs.

drills.q: A candidate implements Rotate List (LC61) by reversing the whole list, reversing the first k nodes, reversing the rest, and reversing the whole thing again (the array-rotation triple-reversal trick). Is this the right tool for a linked list, and why or why not?
drills.a: It's unnecessary complexity. Triple reversal is a trick specifically for in-place ARRAY rotation, where you can't easily jump to an arbitrary position without shifting elements. A linked list lets you directly relink three pointers once you know the new head/tail boundary: compute k mod length, walk to the new tail (at position length-k-1) and new head (right after it), connect the old tail to the old head to form a temporary cycle, then break that cycle at the new boundary -- no reversal of any kind is needed.

drills.q: Explain why reversing a doubly linked list is structurally simpler than reversing a singly linked list, and what the algorithm looks like.
drills.a: A singly linked node only knows its next, so overwriting next without saving it first loses the path forward -- hence the three-pointer technique. A doubly linked node also knows its prev, so even after next is rewritten, the node retains a way back via what was its prev pointer. The algorithm is: for every node, swap its next and prev references; after the full pass, swap the list's head and tail pointers. No prev/curr/next_temp walk is required because nothing is ever lost.

drills.q: A production service uses recursive reversal on a linked list representing a user's action history, and starts throwing stack overflow errors for power users with very long histories. Diagnose the failure and propose the fix without changing the algorithm's correctness.
drills.a: Recursive reversal allocates one stack frame per node before any rewiring begins (it recurses to the tail first), so a history list with tens of thousands of entries can exceed the runtime's default recursion depth (e.g. Python's default limit of 1000 frames, or a JVM/Go goroutine's stack size limit under sufficiently deep recursion). The fix is to replace the recursive implementation with the iterative three-pointer version, which performs the exact same pointer rewrites and produces an identical result, but uses O(1) stack space regardless of list length -- no algorithmic change, only a change in how the same logic is expressed.
